The People's Constitution: Why America Must Abolish the Undemocratic Supreme Court and Restore Power to the People

For over two centuries, a small cabal of nine unelected, life-tenured judges has held the ultimate power to override the will of the American people and their elected representatives. This institution, the United States Supreme Court, operating under the illegitimate doctrine of judicial review, constitutes the single greatest threat to genuine democracy in the United States today. It is time for a radical, necessary, and long-overdue restoration of popular sovereignty: we must abolish the Supreme Court and eliminate judicial review entirely, returning the sacred duty of constitutional interpretation exclusively to the hands of the people's elected representatives or the people themselves through direct democracy. This is not a proposal born of mere dissatisfaction, but of a profound commitment to the core republican principle that the people, through their chosen representatives, must be the final arbiters of their own governance.

The fundamental flaw of the Supreme Court lies in its inherent, unaccountable anti-democracy. The Constitution, the foundational compact of our Republic, derives its "authority from the consent of the governed." Yet, the Supreme Court, populated by justices selected through partisan political maneuvers (often by presidents rejected by the popular vote) and confirmed by a Senate representing vastly unequal populations, operates utterly beyond the reach of that consent. They are not voted on, cannot be recalled, face no term limits, and serve for life – a model more fitting for medieval monarchs than modern citizens. When this unaccountable body declares acts of Congress, state legislatures, or popular initiatives "unconstitutional," it substitutes the subjective judgment of nine elites for the expressed will of millions. This is not law; it is judicial fiat disguised as constitutional interpretation. Consider landmark cases: Dred Scott (denying citizenship to Black Americans), Plessy v. Ferguson (sanctioning Jim Crow), Korematsu (upholding Japanese internment) – these were not victories for liberty, but stark examples of unelected judges imposing catastrophic, morally abhorrent errors on the nation, shielded from correction by the democratic process. Judicial review grants these errors the aura of finality, freezing injustice in constitutional amber. If the people, through their representatives, had the final say, such abominations could have been legislatively reversed far sooner, as the moral consensus evolved.

Proponents of the status quo cling to judicial review as a necessary "check" on majority tyranny. This argument is not only historically dubious – the Framers explicitly rejected a powerful national judiciary as a potential threat, intending Congress to be the primary constitutional interpreter – but it is dangerously cynical and self-defeating in practice. It assumes the people and their elected representatives are inherently untrustworthy guardians of rights, while simultaneously elevating an unelected elite above reproach. The reality is that the Court itself is frequently the instrument of minority tyranny or elite preference. Decisions like Citizens United, imposing a radical libertarian interpretation of the First Amendment that drowned elections in corporate cash against overwhelming bipartisan public opposition, or Shelby County, dismantling core Voting Rights Act protections despite clear Congressional findings of ongoing discrimination, demonstrate how the Court actively enables tyranny – the tyranny of powerful interests and partisan majorities on the Court itself. The "tyranny of the majority" is a phantom menace constantly invoked to justify judicial usurpation, while the very real tyranny of the unaccountable few on the bench operates daily. True protection for minorities arises not from cloistered judges, but from robust democratic processes that foster dialogue, build supermajorities for rights, and allow for continuous legislative refinement – mechanisms impossible under a system where a narrow Court majority can slam the door permanently.

Furthermore, concentrating ultimate constitutional power in the Supreme Court stifles vital democratic development and fosters corrosive political polarization. Every presidential election becomes a de facto referendum on Supreme Court vacancies, poisoning the political well for decades. Major policy questions – from healthcare to gun control to reproductive rights – are yanked out of the legislative arena, where compromise, constituent pressure, and evidence-based debate can occur, and dumped onto the Court's doorstep. This transforms the judiciary into the ultimate political battleground, eroding public trust in all branches of government. When the people know their elected representatives' efforts can be nullified by nine judges, it breeds cynicism and disengagement. Democracy withers when the people believe their votes don't truly matter because unelected judges hold the final trump card. Returning constitutional interpretation to Congress or state legislatures, or even to the people via referendum on specific constitutional questions, would revitalize representative democracy. Debates about constitutional meaning would occur openly, with legislators accountable to voters, allowing for evolving interpretations reflecting contemporary values and needs. It would force proponents of rights to build genuine political consensus, making those rights more deeply rooted and sustainable than any judicial pronouncement.

"But won't this lead to rights being trampled by popular whim?" This is the predictable, yet ultimately hollow, fearmongering of judicial elitists. The Constitution, as amended (especially by the Reconstruction Amendments), establishes a robust floor of fundamental rights. Congress, precisely because it is accountable, has proven far more reliable than the Court in expanding and protecting rights. Consider the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Voting Rights Act of 1965, the Americans with Disabilities Act – transformative legislation enacted democratically that the Court, left to its own devices for decades, had utterly failed to secure. Elected representatives, facing the voters, are more responsive to shifting social mores and the demands of marginalized groups than insulated justices. Moreover, a system where constitutional amendments or major rights interpretations require supermajorities in Congress (or popular supermajorities via referendum) provides a more legitimate and durable check against transient majoritarian excesses than the arbitrary rulings of nine individuals. The Founders provided the amendment process for a reason – it is the democratic path for constitutional evolution, deliberately difficult but ultimately controlled by the people's representatives. Judicial review usurped this path.

Some may point to other democracies with constitutional courts, but the United States is unique in the sheer, unreviewable power it grants its Supreme Court. Most other systems feature parliamentary supremacy (like the UK), where legislatures retain ultimate authority, or constitutional courts with more balanced structures and clearer limitations (like Germany's). The US model is an extreme outlier, concentrating near-absolute interpretive power in an unaccountable body – an anomaly incompatible with modern democratic principles.

The time for timid reform is over. Tinkering with term limits or court-packing merely accepts the flawed premise of judicial supremacy. The deep rot lies in the very concept of unelected judges possessing the final, unassailable authority to define the nation's highest law. Abolishing the Supreme Court and eliminating judicial review is not an attack on the Constitution; it is the only way to fulfill the Constitution's true promise of "We the People." It is a return to the core republican ideal that the people, through the representatives they elect or through their own direct voice on fundamental questions, must hold the reins of ultimate sovereignty. It will force our political system to mature, to resolve its deepest conflicts through the difficult, messy, but ultimately legitimate work of democratic politics, rather than hidden deliberations behind closed doors. It will restore accountability, revitalize civic engagement, and ensure that the Constitution lives and breathes as an expression of the popular will, not the ossified doctrine of a privileged few. The Crowned Heads of Black-robed Tyranny must be dethroned. The Constitution belongs to the people. It is time to take it back.

Proposed Abolition of the U.S. Supreme Court & Judicial Review: Stated Arguments and Purported Benefits (Neutral Explanation)

It is important to preface this by stating that abolishing the U.S. Supreme Court and the principle of judicial review is an extremely radical and non-mainstream proposal within contemporary U.S. constitutional discourse. No major political party or significant constitutional movement currently advocates for complete abolition. The arguments below represent theoretical critiques and proposals put forward by some legal scholars, political theorists, or activists who view the current system as fundamentally flawed. This explanation aims for neutrality, presenting these stated reasons and purported benefits without endorsement.

Core Critique Underpinning the Proposal

Proponents of abolition argue that the core flaw lies in "the counter-majoritarian difficulty" – the idea that unelected, politically insulated judges possess the ultimate authority to invalidate laws passed by democratically elected representatives (Congress, state legislatures) and signed by elected executives. They contend this violates the principle of popular sovereignty and democratic self-governance, as the Constitution's meaning is effectively decided by a small, unaccountable body for generations.

Stated Reasons for Abolishing Judicial Review & the Supreme Court

  1. Democratic Deficit: The primary argument is that constitutional interpretation should be, and historically was intended to be, primarily a political and legislative process. Proponents cite:

    • Founding Era Practice: Early debates (e.g., Jefferson, some Anti-Federalists) viewed all branches (including Congress) as having co-equal duty and authority to interpret the Constitution in their actions.
    • Lack of Explicit Grant: Critics note Marbury v. Madison (1803), which established judicial review, derived this power from implication ("it is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is"), not an explicit constitutional grant. They argue this usurped power from the political branches.
    • Life Tenure & Insulation: Justices serve for life, are not subject to election or recall, and lack direct accountability to the public whose lives their rulings profoundly impact. This, critics argue, creates a permanent, unresponsive elite.

  2. Judicial Activism/Overreach: Critics allege that the Court frequently makes policy decisions under the guise of constitutional interpretation, effectively legislating from the bench. Abolition, they argue, would force contentious social and political issues back into the democratic arena where elected representatives must directly debate, compromise, and take responsibility for outcomes.

  3. Lack of Legitimacy & Transparency: Decisions are made by a secretive conference, based on complex legal reasoning often inaccessible to the public, without mechanisms for direct democratic correction beyond the arduous constitutional amendment process. Proponents argue this fosters public distrust and perceptions of illegitimacy, especially for highly polarized 5-4 rulings.

  4. Stagnation of Constitutional Meaning: Critics argue judicial review freezes constitutional interpretation based on the views of long-dead Justices or historical contexts vastly different from the present. They contend a democratic process would allow the Constitution's meaning to evolve more fluidly and directly in response to contemporary societal values and needs.

Purported Benefits of Replacing with Democratic Mechanisms

Proponents argue replacing judicial review with democratic processes would:

  1. Increase Democratic Accountability: Final constitutional interpretation would reside with bodies directly answerable to voters (e.g., Congress, state legislatures via conventions, or new elected bodies). Elected officials would have to openly debate and justify their interpretation of the Constitution when making laws, owning the consequences politically.
  2. Enhance Popular Sovereignty: The ultimate authority over the nation's founding document would reside with the people, exercised through their elected representatives or direct democratic processes, aligning more closely with the principle that "the people are the rightful masters of both Congress and the courts."
  3. Promote Political Compromise and Debate: Forcing constitutional questions into the political arena would require lawmakers to negotiate, build coalitions, and find pragmatic solutions acceptable to a majority (or supermajority), fostering a more robust and transparent political process.
  4. Increase Transparency and Understandability: Constitutional debates would happen in open legislative sessions or public conventions, with arguments framed in political and moral terms familiar to citizens, rather than opaque legal doctrine. Voters could more clearly see who is responsible for decisions.
  5. Allow for More Responsive Evolution: The meaning of constitutional principles (like "equal protection" or "due process") could adapt more readily to changing societal understandings through legislative action or constitutional amendments, without waiting for shifts in the Court's composition over decades.

Proposed Democratic Mechanisms (Theoretical)

  • Enhanced Legislative Role: Congress (potentially requiring supermajorities) would have the final say on the constitutionality of its own laws and federal actions. State legislatures might gain stronger roles in interpreting state constitutions or federal powers.
  • Constitutional Conventions: Regularly scheduled or issue-specific conventions with delegates elected by the people to debate and define constitutional meaning or propose amendments for ratification.
  • Elected Constitutional Councils: Creating a new, directly elected body (e.g., a Constitutional Assembly or Council) with specific authority to review laws for constitutionality, subject to electoral accountability.
  • Supermajority Requirements: Requiring supermajorities (e.g., 2/3 or 3/4) in Congress or state legislatures for passing laws affecting fundamental rights, implicitly serving as a constitutional check.
  • Referenda/Initiatives: Allowing citizens to directly vote on the constitutionality of specific laws or broad constitutional interpretations via ballot measures.

Significant Concerns & Counterpoints (Essential for Neutrality)

While explaining the stated arguments for abolition, neutrality requires acknowledging the primary reasons judicial review exists and why abolition is widely opposed:

  • Protection of Minority Rights: The core historical justification for judicial review is protecting minorities from the "tyranny of the majority." Elected branches may lack the will to uphold constitutional rights (e.g., racial minorities, free speech dissenters) against popular majorities. Democratic mechanisms could entrench majoritarian discrimination.
  • Stability and Predictability: Judicial review provides a stable framework for law and expectations. Constant political re-litigation of constitutional meaning could lead to volatility and undermine the rule of law.
  • Expertise and Deliberation: Courts offer (in theory) a forum for reasoned, evidence-based analysis insulated from immediate political pressures and electoral cycles.
  • Structural Safeguards: The difficulty of amending the Constitution (Article V) and Senate confirmation of Justices are themselves democratic checks on the Court, making abolition seem like an overcorrection.
  • Practical Feasibility: Replacing the intricate system of constitutional law developed over 230 years with untested democratic mechanisms is viewed by most experts as legally and politically unworkable and potentially destabilizing.

Conclusion

The proposal to abolish the Supreme Court and judicial review stems from a deep critique of unelected judges holding ultimate constitutional authority, prioritizing democratic accountability and popular sovereignty over judicial restraint. Proponents argue it would return power to elected representatives, foster transparent political debate, and allow the Constitution to evolve democratically. However, this perspective is highly controversial and faces substantial counterarguments centered on the vital role judicial review plays in protecting minority rights, ensuring stable governance, and providing a check against majority overreach – functions widely believed to be inadequately fulfilled by purely political processes alone. The existence of judicial review remains a fundamental, albeit contested, pillar of the U.S. constitutional system.

A Case for Democratic Constitutional Interpretation

Introduction

The United States Supreme Court wields extraordinary power over American life. Nine unelected officials, serving lifetime appointments, can invalidate laws passed by democratically elected representatives and block policies supported by overwhelming majorities. This essay examines arguments for reconsidering this arrangement and exploring more democratic alternatives for constitutional interpretation.

The Democratic Deficit Argument

Unelected power: Supreme Court justices are appointed, not elected, and serve until death or retirement. They answer to no constituency and face no accountability at the ballot box.

Counter-majoritarian difficulty: The Court regularly overturns laws passed by elected legislators who directly represent the people. This creates tension with basic democratic principles.

Generational lock-in: Justices appointed decades ago make decisions binding on current generations who had no voice in their selection.

Historical Concerns with Judicial Review

Not explicitly constitutional: Judicial review isn't mentioned in the Constitution itself—it was established by the Court in Marbury v. Madison (1803), essentially a self-granted power.

Historical errors: The Court has made catastrophic mistakes:

  • Dred Scott (1857) denied citizenship to Black Americans
  • Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) upheld segregation
  • Korematsu (1944) approved Japanese internment
  • Lochner era cases blocked worker protections

These weren't simply wrong interpretations—they caused immense human suffering and impeded democratic progress.

The Political Reality

Here are the main arguments that critics of the U.S. Supreme Court and of judicial review advance when they propose abolishing or sharply reducing the Court’s powers, and replacing them with more democratic mechanisms of constitutional interpretation. This is a summary of that perspective, not an endorsement.

1. Democratic Legitimacy and Accountability

a. Unelected, life-tenured judges

Critics argue that it is undemocratic for nine unelected, life-tenured justices to have final authority over the meaning of the Constitution and the validity of laws passed by elected representatives.

  • Members of Congress and presidents can be removed through elections.
  • Justices cannot easily be removed and face no regular electoral check.
  • This is said to concentrate enormous power in a small, unaccountable group.

b. Counter-majoritarian difficulty

Judicial review can allow a small number of judges to overturn laws supported by majorities at both the federal and state level. Opponents see this as a “counter-majoritarian” institution that can:

  • Thwart democratic decisions.
  • Entrench minority preferences against popular will.
  • Freeze certain policy areas outside of democratic contestation.

They argue that, in a democracy, the people—through legislatures and other broad-based processes—should be the ultimate interpreters of the constitution.

2. Political and Ideological Capture

a. Partisan appointments

Because justices are appointed by presidents and confirmed by the Senate, critics see the Court as:

  • Deeply shaped by partisan politics rather than neutral reason.
  • Reflecting the ideological balance of a few pivotal electoral moments rather than ongoing public opinion.

They argue that:

  • The timing of vacancies, election outcomes, and Senate composition can give one party outsized long-term control over constitutional meaning.
  • This can “lock in” a particular ideology for decades, even as public opinion changes.

b. Judicial activism and policymaking

Critics say the modern Court often acts as a policymaker:

  • Striking down or reworking legislation.
  • Setting broad social policy in areas like campaign finance, voting rights, reproductive rights, and administrative regulation.

From this perspective, the Court is not merely interpreting law but actively making law, which critics think should be done by elected bodies.

3. Elitism and Social Bias

a. Socioeconomic and professional homogeneity

Opponents note that most justices come from narrow social and professional backgrounds:

  • Elite law schools.
  • Prior service on appellate courts.
  • Similar professional networks.

They argue that such a body:

  • Is not representative of the population.
  • May systematically favor the interests and perspectives of elites, corporations, or particular social groups.

b. Historical record of controversial decisions

Critics point to decisions that, in retrospect, are widely seen as unjust or harmful:

  • Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) upholding slavery-related positions.
  • Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) upholding segregation.
  • Korematsu v. United States (1944) upholding internment of Japanese Americans.
  • More recent rulings viewed by critics as entrenching inequality or limiting democratic participation.

They argue that judicial review has no consistent record of being more protective of rights or justice than democratic institutions; sometimes it has reinforced oppression.

4. Constitutional Indeterminacy and Judicial Discretion

a. Ambiguous constitutional text

The Constitution is often vague or written at a high level of generality (e.g., “due process,” “equal protection,” “cruel and unusual punishment”). Critics argue:

  • There is no single “correct” legal answer in many cases.
  • Judicial decisions often reflect values and ideology rather than neutral deduction.

If interpretation unavoidably involves value judgments, opponents ask why those judgments should be made by judges instead of the public through democratic processes.

b. The myth of “neutral” interpretation

From this viewpoint, claims of purely neutral or mechanical interpretation are seen as:

  • Masking the real power of justices to choose among plausible interpretations.
  • Providing an aura of legal inevitability to what are essentially political or moral choices.

Abolishing or curbing judicial review, and shifting interpretation to more democratic bodies, is argued to make this value-choice aspect more transparent and accountable.

5. Institutional Problems and Structural Concerns

a. Overconcentration of power

With strong-form judicial review, the Supreme Court can:

  • Invalidate federal and state laws.
  • Shape national policy with decisions that are difficult to reverse absent constitutional amendment (which is very hard to achieve).

Critics see this as excessive centralization of constitutional authority.

b. Lack of effective correction mechanisms

There are very few ways to respond to decisions that a broad majority views as wrong:

  • Constitutional amendments are rare and difficult.
  • Court-packing or jurisdiction-stripping are extreme and politically explosive tools.

By contrast, legislative and executive decisions can be altered with each election cycle. Critics suggest this makes democratic institutions more adaptable and responsive than a powerful, entrenched high court.

6. Alternative Democratic Models of Constitutional Interpretation

Proposals to abolish or significantly reduce the role of the Supreme Court usually come with suggestions for more democratic mechanisms. Common ideas include:

a. Parliamentary or legislative supremacy

Under this model:

  • The elected legislature has final authority over constitutional meaning.
  • Courts may still interpret statutes and resolve ordinary disputes, but cannot strike down statutes as unconstitutional.
  • If a law is unpopular or seen as rights-violating, voters can replace legislators.

Supporters argue that this maximizes democratic control and keeps ultimate authority with the people’s representatives.

b. “Weak-form” judicial review

Inspired by some other democracies (e.g., the UK, Canada, New Zealand), critics of the U.S. system sometimes propose:

  • Courts may issue “declarations of inconsistency” or “incompatibility” with constitutional principles or rights.
  • Legislatures then decide whether to revise the law, override the court, or accept the declaration.
  • The final word remains with the democratic branches, not the judiciary.

This is seen as a compromise that preserves expert legal input but avoids judicial supremacy.

c. Popular constitutionalism

Advocates of “popular constitutionalism” argue that:

  • Constitutional meaning should emerge from broad public debate, social movements, and electoral politics.
  • Social groups, activists, and political parties should interpret and contest constitutional principles in public, rather than relying on courts.

Institutionally, this might involve:

  • Constitutional referendums on contested questions.
  • Citizen assemblies or deliberative bodies that interpret or propose constitutional norms.
  • Requirements that major constitutional changes or rights limitations be approved directly by the electorate.

d. Multi-branch interpretive responsibility

Some reformers argue that each branch of government should interpret the Constitution for itself:

  • Congress interprets when passing laws.
  • The President interprets when signing or vetoing laws, or when enforcing them.
  • Courts interpret in the course of deciding cases, but their views are not uniquely authoritative.

Abolishing strong-form judicial review would, in this model, prevent courts from unilaterally invalidating acts of the other branches, and constitutional meaning would be a continuing, multi-institutional dialogue.

7. Rights Protection Through Democracy Rather Than Courts

A central defense of judicial review is that it protects minority rights against majority abuses. Critics respond with several counterpoints:

a. Democratic processes can protect rights

They argue that:

  • Rights protections can be entrenched in the political culture, parties’ platforms, civil society, and ordinary legislation.
  • Elected officials sometimes expand rights more rapidly than courts (for example, through civil rights statutes, voting rights acts, or anti-discrimination laws).

From this view, rights are more secure when grounded in broad political support than when dependent on interpretations by a small court that can change in composition.

b. Courts are not consistently pro-rights

Opponents note:

  • Courts have sometimes curtailed rights or upheld repressive policies.
  • What counts as a “right” is often contested, and courts may favor some interests (e.g., property or corporate rights) over others (e.g., labor or social rights).

They conclude that judicial review does not reliably favor the vulnerable; it just shifts power to different elites.

8. Transparency and Public Engagement

a. Making constitutional politics explicit

Critics claim that strong judicial review:

  • Moves fundamental value disputes into legal-technical forums.
  • Frames issues as technical legal questions rather than open political choices.

By abolishing or limiting judicial review:

  • Constitutional conflict becomes more openly political and participatory.
  • Citizens, parties, and movements must argue their positions to the electorate rather than to a small group of judges.

b. Encouraging civic responsibility

If the public cannot rely on courts to “fix” unconstitutional laws, critics argue that:

  • Citizens may feel a stronger responsibility to engage, vote, organize, and hold officials accountable.
  • Constitutional culture becomes something the public actively shapes, not something “handed down” by a court.

9. Practical Proposals for Replacement Mechanisms

Specific abolitionist or radical reform proposals vary, but they often combine several elements:

  • Remove or sharply restrict the Supreme Court’s power to strike down legislation.
  • Transform the Court into:
    • A court of final appeal on ordinary legal questions only; or
    • A purely advisory constitutional body whose opinions can be overridden by legislatures.
  • Strengthen democratic checks, such as:
    • Easier constitutional amendment processes.
    • Requirements that major rights-related laws be reaffirmed by referendums or supermajorities.
    • Enhanced protections for political participation (voting rights, party competition, independent election administration).
  • Create more representative institutions to handle constitutional questions, such as:
    • Citizen assemblies with randomly selected members.
    • Periodic constitutional conventions elected by the people.

The unifying goal is to move final constitutional authority from a small judicial elite to institutions that are directly or more broadly accountable to the public.

10. Summary of the Rationale

In condensed form, proponents of abolishing or sharply limiting the U.S. Supreme Court and judicial review argue:

  • Constitutional interpretation is inherently political and value-laden, not purely technical.
  • In a democracy, ultimate political authority should rest with institutions accountable to the people, not life-tenured judges.
  • The Supreme Court has a mixed historical record on justice and rights, and its structure encourages partisan capture and elite bias.
  • Strong-form judicial review centralizes power, weakens public responsibility, and can impede democratic self-government.
  • Democratic mechanisms—legislative supremacy, weak-form review, referendums, citizen assemblies, and popular constitutionalism—could distribute constitutional authority more broadly and make it more responsive to evolving public values.

These are the main lines of argument advanced by those who favor abolishing or greatly reducing the role of the Supreme Court in constitutional interpretation, in favor of more democratic alternatives.

Model Response:

Reclaiming Democratic Sovereignty: The Case for Abolishing Judicial Supremacy

Introduction

The United States Supreme Court, once envisioned as the "least dangerous branch" of government, has evolved into an unelected super-legislature that routinely overrides the will of the people and their elected representatives. The principle of judicial review—nowhere explicitly stated in the Constitution—has transformed nine unelected lawyers into the ultimate arbiters of American law and social policy. This anti-democratic arrangement violates fundamental principles of popular sovereignty and representative government. The time has come to abolish the Supreme Court's power of judicial review and return constitutional interpretation to the people and their elected representatives, where it rightfully belongs.

The Democratic Deficit of Judicial Supremacy

The Undemocratic Nature of Life Tenure

The Supreme Court represents a profound anomaly in American democracy. While we pride ourselves on government "of the people, by the people, for the people," we have surrendered ultimate governmental authority to nine individuals who never face election, serve for life, and answer to no one. These justices, appointed through an increasingly partisan process and confirmed by senators representing a minority of the population, wield veto power over any law passed by democratically elected legislatures.

Consider the absurdity: a single justice, appointed decades ago by a long-dead president, can nullify legislation supported by hundreds of current legislators representing millions of contemporary voters. Justice Clarence Thomas, appointed in 1991, continues to shape American law more than three decades later, long after the president who appointed him left office and died. This is not democracy; it is rule by the dead hand of the past.

Lack of Accountability Mechanisms

Unlike every other governmental official in our system, Supreme Court justices face virtually no accountability. Presidents can be impeached and removed; they also face voters every four years. Members of Congress must regularly return to their constituents for approval. Even federal judges below the Supreme Court level can have their decisions overturned by higher courts. But Supreme Court justices, once confirmed, become answerable to no one but themselves.

The impeachment process, theoretically available, has proven utterly ineffective. Only one justice has ever been impeached (Samuel Chase in 1804), and he was acquitted. The bar for removal—"high crimes and misdemeanors"—sets an impossibly high standard that excludes ideological extremism, judicial activism, or simple incompetence. Justices who become senile, out-of-touch, or physically incapable can cling to power until death, as witnessed repeatedly throughout American history.

The Manufactured Power of Judicial Review

Historical Illegitimacy

The power of judicial review finds no explicit authorization in the Constitution's text. The Founders, who carefully enumerated powers throughout the document, somehow forgot to mention that the Supreme Court could invalidate laws? This glaring omission was no accident. Many framers explicitly rejected judicial supremacy. Thomas Jefferson warned that judicial review would make the Constitution "a mere thing of wax in the hands of the judiciary."

The Court essentially granted itself this power in Marbury v. Madison (1803), a breathtaking act of judicial self-aggrandizement. Chief Justice John Marshall, acting in a case where he had a clear conflict of interest, manufactured a power nowhere granted by the people or their representatives. Every exercise of judicial review since then rests on this illegitimate foundation—a constitutional coup that succeeded only because it wasn't immediately challenged.

The Myth of Legal Expertise

Defenders of judicial review claim judges possess special expertise in constitutional interpretation. This is nonsense. Constitutional interpretation involves moral, philosophical, and political judgments, not technical legal skills. When the Court decides whether abortion, same-sex marriage, or gun rights receive constitutional protection, it makes fundamentally political decisions about values and social policy.

Why should nine lawyers have superior insight into these questions than 535 elected representatives or 330 million citizens? Many constitutional provisions—"equal protection," "due process," "cruel and unusual punishment"—are deliberately vague, inviting interpretation based on contemporary values. These are precisely the questions democracy exists to resolve through deliberation and voting, not judicial decree.

Historical Harm: The Court's Record of Injustice

Protecting Oppression

Throughout American history, the Supreme Court has more often protected injustice than advanced justice. Consider its most consequential decisions:

  • Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) declared Black Americans could never be citizens and helped precipitate the Civil War
  • Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) legitimized racial segregation for nearly 60 years
  • Lochner v. New York (1905) and its progeny struck down worker protections, minimum wage laws, and child labor restrictions for decades
  • Korematsu v. United States (1944) upheld Japanese internment camps
  • Citizens United v. FEC (2010) opened floodgates of corporate money in politics

For every celebrated decision like Brown v. Board of Education, there are dozens of cases where the Court blocked social progress, protected privileged interests, and frustrated democratic reform. The Court has consistently lagged behind public opinion on questions of justice and equality, serving as a brake on progress rather than an engine of advancement.

Inconsistency and Political Bias

The Court's supposed commitment to neutral legal principles is a transparent fiction. Justices routinely abandon their stated interpretive philosophies when convenient, revealing that constitutional interpretation is simply politics by other means. "Originalist" justices discover new rights when it suits conservative policy preferences (see District of Columbia v. Heller on gun rights) while "living constitutionalist" justices suddenly become strict textualists when defending preferred outcomes.

The Court's legitimacy crisis has become undeniable. Public approval ratings have plummeted as Americans recognize what legal realists have long known: justices are politicians in robes, advancing partisan agendas while hiding behind legal jargon. When Supreme Court nominations become the most consequential political prizes, triggering massive political warfare, we must acknowledge that the Court is a political institution requiring democratic accountability.

The Superior Democratic Alternative

Legislative Constitutional Interpretation

Elected representatives, not appointed judges, should determine constitutional meaning. Congress and state legislatures, directly accountable to voters, better reflect contemporary values and can adjust their interpretations as society evolves. This isn't radical—many democratic nations, including the United Kingdom, Netherlands, and New Zealand, function successfully without judicial review.

Under this system, Congress would establish committees dedicated to constitutional compliance, reviewing proposed legislation for consistency with constitutional text and principles. Representatives would debate constitutional meaning openly, allowing public participation in these crucial decisions. Voters dissatisfied with their representatives' constitutional interpretations could replace them at the next election—a democratic check entirely absent from judicial review.

Constitutional interpretation would become a regular part of democratic discourse, not an arcane practice monopolized by legal priests. Citizens would engage more deeply with their founding document, understanding that they, not distant judges, bear responsibility for its meaning.

Popular Constitutional Review

For particularly significant constitutional questions, direct popular vote could determine interpretation. Modern technology makes this feasible in ways the Founders couldn't imagine. Switzerland successfully uses referenda for constitutional amendments and major policy decisions, demonstrating that citizens can thoughtfully engage with complex constitutional questions.

Imagine if Americans, not five Supreme Court justices, had decided whether corporations are "persons" with free speech rights, whether the Second Amendment protects individual gun ownership, or whether the Constitution guarantees abortion rights. These democratic determinations would carry far greater legitimacy than judicial edicts imposed by an unelected council.

States could experiment with different models of popular review. Some might require supermajorities for certain interpretations, others might use ranked-choice voting to find consensus positions. This experimentation would invigorate constitutional democracy rather than freezing it under judicial monopoly.

Addressing Counterarguments

The "Tyranny of the Majority" Objection

Critics warn that abolishing judicial review would enable majority tyranny, allowing democratic majorities to trample minority rights. This fear is overblown and historically inaccurate. First, the Supreme Court has often been the instrument of oppression, not its opponent. From Dred Scott to Plessy to the gutting of the Voting Rights Act, the Court has frequently failed to protect vulnerable minorities.

Second, democratic institutions have proven capable of protecting rights without judicial supervision. Legislative bodies passed the Civil Rights Act, the Voting Rights Act, and the Americans with Disabilities Act—often over judicial resistance. Many nations without judicial review maintain stronger protections for minorities than the United States.

Third, alternative mechanisms can protect against majoritarian excess. Supermajority requirements for certain actions, federalism allowing different approaches in different states, and strong democratic norms all constrain majority power. These democratic safeguards are preferable to elite rule by unelected judges.

The "Stability and Predictability" Argument

Defenders claim judicial review provides legal stability and predictability essential for economic and social planning. Yet the Court regularly overturns precedent when its composition changes, creating massive uncertainty. Businesses and individuals can hardly rely on constitutional interpretations that shift with each new appointment.

Democratic interpretation would actually increase predictability by tying constitutional meaning to observable public opinion and electoral results. Rather than waiting anxiously to see how a new justice might vote, Americans would know that constitutional interpretation reflects contemporary democratic consensus.

The "Protection of Unpopular Rights" Defense

Some argue courts must protect unpopular rights that democratic majorities would eliminate. But this assumes judges are more enlightened than citizens—a fundamentally anti-democratic premise. Moreover, genuinely unpopular rights rarely survive judicial protection anyway. Brown v. Board succeeded only because it aligned with shifting public opinion and federal enforcement. Roe v. Wade, conversely, generated decades of backlash and was ultimately overturned.

Rights are most secure when they enjoy democratic support, not when they depend on judicial protection. Marriage equality gained lasting acceptance through changing public opinion and legislative action, not merely judicial decree. Democratic deliberation may move slowly, but it builds consensus that judicial imposition cannot achieve.

International Perspectives and Successful Alternatives

Many thriving democracies function without American-style judicial review, demonstrating its dispensability. The United Kingdom Parliament holds ultimate authority over constitutional interpretation. The Netherlands explicitly prohibits courts from reviewing the constitutionality of statutes. New Zealand courts can declare laws inconsistent with rights, but Parliament retains final say.

These nations haven't descended into tyranny or chaos. Indeed, they often protect rights more effectively than the United States. They maintain independent judiciaries that interpret and apply laws without claiming supremacy over democratic institutions. Their examples prove that democracy can flourish—even thrive—without judicial supremacy.

Canada's "notwithstanding clause" offers another model, allowing legislatures to override certain judicial decisions for renewable five-year periods. This compromise preserves judicial input while maintaining democratic supremacy. Such mechanisms could ease America's transition away from judicial review.

The Path Forward: Implementation

Gradual Transition

Abolishing judicial review need not happen overnight. Congress could begin by restricting the Court's jurisdiction over certain subjects, as the Constitution explicitly permits. Starting with areas where the Court has proven most problematic—campaign finance, voting rights, economic regulation—would build momentum for broader reform.

Simultaneously, Congress and state legislatures should develop institutional capacity for constitutional interpretation. Creating dedicated constitutional committees, hiring constitutional scholars, and establishing procedures for constitutional review would prepare democratic institutions to assume this responsibility.

Constitutional Amendment

Ultimately, a constitutional amendment should formalize the abolition of judicial review and establish democratic alternatives. This amendment should:

  1. Explicitly deny federal courts the power to invalidate democratically enacted laws
  2. Establish procedures for legislative constitutional review
  3. Create mechanisms for popular constitutional interpretation
  4. Define limited circumstances where judicial input remains advisory
  5. Provide transition procedures to prevent legal chaos

The amendment process itself would generate crucial democratic deliberation about constitutional interpretation, engaging Americans in fundamental questions about self-government.

Building Democratic Culture

Successfully replacing judicial review requires strengthening democratic culture and institutions. Civic education must improve, ensuring citizens understand constitutional principles and their role in interpretation. Media coverage of constitutional issues should expand beyond Supreme Court drama to include democratic deliberation.

Political parties should develop clear constitutional philosophies, making constitutional interpretation a regular electoral issue. Voters would learn to evaluate candidates' constitutional views alongside their policy positions. This democratic engagement would revitalize American constitutionalism.

Conclusion: Reclaiming Popular Sovereignty

The American experiment in self-government has been hijacked by nine unelected lawyers wielding power never granted by the people. The Supreme Court's assumed supremacy over constitutional interpretation contradicts basic democratic principles and concentrates dangerous power in unaccountable hands. History demonstrates that the Court has more often frustrated justice than advanced it, protecting privilege and blocking progress behind a veil of legal mysticism.

The alternative—democratic constitutional interpretation—would reinvigorate American democracy by returning fundamental decisions to the people and their representatives. Whether through legislative review, popular referenda, or innovative combinations, democratic mechanisms can interpret our Constitution while maintaining accountability to contemporary citizens rather than dead framers or life-tenured elites.

Other democracies thrive without judicial review. American democracy survived and even flourished during periods when the Court exercised this power sparingly. We need not accept judicial supremacy as inevitable or desirable. The Constitution belongs to the living, not to nine robed rulers.

The time has come to complete the democratic revolution the Founders began. Just as they rejected monarchy and aristocracy, we must reject judicial supremacy. The principle that legitimate government derives from consent of the governed demands that constitutional interpretation return to the people. Only then can we truly claim to live in a democracy where the people, not judges, are sovereign.

Abolishing judicial review won't be easy. Entrenched interests benefit from the current system, and change always faces resistance. But the promise of genuine democratic self-government—where citizens shape their fundamental law through democratic participation rather than hoping for favorable judicial appointments—justifies the effort. We must have the courage to trust democracy with democracy itself.

The choice is clear: continue accepting rule by an unelected judicial aristocracy or reclaim popular sovereignty over our Constitution. For those who truly believe in democracy, the answer is obvious. The Supreme Court's stranglehold on constitutional interpretation must end. The Constitution must return to the people. Judicial review, established in Marbury v. Madison (1803), was a self-asserted power by the Court, absent from constitutional text. Thomas Jefferson warned of judicial overreach, stating, "The Constitution is a mere thing of wax in the hands of the judiciary."   1. Undemocratic Structure: Justices, appointed for life, face no electoral accountability.   3. Stagnation vs. Progress: Lifetime tenure insulates justices from societal change. While public opinion evolved on issues like marriage equality, the Court lagged until Obergefell v. Hodges (2015), delaying civil rights progress.

Benefits of Elected Interpretation
Transitioning constitutional interpretation to elected representatives or popular vote offers transformative advantages:

  1. Accountability: Legislators, answerable to voters, must justify interpretations or face electoral consequences. This aligns governance with contemporary values, as seen in New Zealand’s parliamentary sovereignty model, where elected bodies adapt laws without judicial override.

Introduction

The Undemocratic Foundations of the Supreme Court

At its core, the Supreme Court represents an affront to democratic principles. The Framers of the Constitution envisioned a government "of the people, by the people, for the people," yet they created a judicial branch insulated from public accountability. Justices are appointed by the president and confirmed by the Senate, but once seated, they serve for life, immune to elections, recalls, or even the shifting tides of public opinion. This structure allows a handful of individuals—often ideologically extreme and out of touch with modern society—to nullify laws passed by Congress or state legislatures, effectively vetoing the democratic process.

Such decisions underscore how judicial review empowers an elite minority to thwart the democratic majority, perpetuating inequality and eroding trust in government. Abolishing the Court would eliminate this imbalance, ensuring that no unelected body can hijack the people's sovereignty.

The Illegitimate Origins of Judicial Review

Judicial review is often portrayed as a foundational pillar of American governance, but this is a myth perpetuated by judicial apologists. The Constitution nowhere explicitly grants the Supreme Court the authority to declare laws unconstitutional. Article III merely establishes the judiciary and outlines its jurisdiction, without mentioning the power to invalidate acts of Congress or the executive. This authority was invented by Chief Justice John Marshall in Marbury v. Madison, a case where the Court conveniently expanded its own power while resolving a political dispute. Marshall's reasoning—that it is "emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is"—was a bold power grab, unsupported by the text or intent of the Framers.

Shifting to a system of elected or popular constitutional interpretation offers profound benefits. Fears of chaos are exaggerated; countries without judicial review, like the Netherlands, maintain stable democracies. Transitional mechanisms, such as phasing out the Court over a decade, could ease the shift, preserving stability while embracing democracy.

The United States Supreme Court and judicial review represent an outdated, undemocratic barrier to true self-governance. By abolishing them and empowering elected representatives or popular votes to interpret the Constitution, we can reclaim our democracy, ensuring that power resides with the people, not an elite judiciary. Let us abolish the Court, eliminate judicial review, and build a more accountable, vibrant republic—one where the Constitution serves the people, not the other way around. Introduction

In the American political imagination, the Supreme Court is often revered as the guardian of the Constitution, an impartial arbiter standing above the fray of partisan politics. When nine unelected, life-tenured justices possess the final authority to nullify laws passed by elected representatives, the principle of self-government is compromised. To truly realize the promise of democracy enshrined in the phrase "We the People," the United States must abolish the Supreme Court as the final arbiter of constitutional meaning and eliminate the doctrine of judicial review. The Democratic Deficit

The primary argument against the current system is the undemocratic nature of judicial supremacy. In a republic, legitimacy flows from the consent of the governed. Members of Congress and the President must face the electorate at regular intervals; they are accountable for their decisions. In contrast, Supreme Court Justices are appointed for life, insulated from public opinion and electoral consequence. When the Court strikes down legislation, it overrides the will of the majority as expressed through their representatives. This creates a "democratic deficit," where critical moral and political decisions—regarding healthcare, voting rights, or economic regulation—are removed from the public sphere and decided in the closed chambers of the judiciary. By abolishing the Court's power of judicial review, we restore the capacity of the people to govern themselves, accepting that in a democracy, the right to make mistakes belongs to the electorate, not to a panel of legal elites.

Historical Legitimacy and Marbury v. Madison

Proponents of the status quo often argue that judicial review is an essential feature of the Constitution. Historically, this is incorrect. The Constitution does not explicitly grant the Supreme Court the power to declare acts of Congress unconstitutional. This power was seized by the Court itself in the 1803 case Marbury v. Madison. From the founding era through the Civil War, the dominance of judicial review was far from settled. Thomas Jefferson argued that allowing judges to be the ultimate arbiters of the Constitution would make the judiciary a "despotic branch." Abraham Lincoln, in his First Inaugural Address, warned that if the policy of the government upon vital questions is to be irrevocably fixed by the Supreme Court, "the people will have ceased to be their own rulers." Abolishing judicial review is not a radical break from tradition; it is a restoration of the original balance of powers intended by the Framers, where each branch has an equal duty to interpret the Constitution within its own sphere.

Popular Constitutionalism

Replacing judicial supremacy with a system of "popular constitutionalism" offers a more robust framework for liberty. Under this system, elected representatives would have the authority to interpret the Constitution when drafting legislation. If the Executive Branch believes a law is constitutional, they may enforce it. If the Legislature believes it is within their powers, they may pass it. This does not mean the Constitution becomes meaningless; rather, it means that constitutional disputes are resolved through political debate and electoral accountability rather than legal fiat.

If the people disagree with their representatives' constitutional interpretation, they have the ultimate remedy: they can vote them out. This creates a dynamic feedback loop where constitutional meaning evolves alongside societal values. For example, debates over the scope of free speech or the right to privacy are fundamentally moral and political questions. They are best settled in the town hall and the ballot box, where arguments are won on merit and public persuasion, rather than in a courtroom, where they are decided on procedural technicalities and the ideological leanings of appointed judges.

History demonstrates that the Supreme Court is often an obstacle to social progress, lagging behind the moral conscience of the nation. In Dred Scott v. The abolition of the Supreme Court's power of judicial review is not an attack on the rule of law; it is an affirmation of the rule of the people. The current system privileges the interpretations of a few unelected individuals over the collective wisdom of the citizenry. By returning constitutional interpretation to the elected branches, the United States would reinvigorate its democracy, ensuring that the Constitution remains a document of the people, by the people, and for the people.   • Legislative override mechanisms.   • Democratic constitutional councils or citizen juries.   • Direct democratic input. More radical proposals envision popular referenda or deliberative polling on specific constitutional controversies, treating constitutional interpretation as a form of high-stakes democratic decision-making akin to amendment or ratification.

The power to say what the Constitution means must reside where sovereignty has always rightfully belonged: with the legislative branch answerable to the people at the ballot box, and with the people themselves through referendum and constitutional amendment.

Some will say this is radical. But radicalism in defense of democracy is no vice! We do not propose chaos. We propose order—the natural order of a self-governing people. Let constitutional questions be decided where they belong: in the House and the Senate, where debate is public, where votes are recorded, where the people can fire their representatives every two or six years. Let the elected President enforce the laws as written, not as five justices divine them to be. Let the states, as laboratories of democracy, craft solutions without fear that a distant tribunal will impose a uniform ideology from above. And where the text is genuinely unclear, let the people amend their Constitution, deliberately and democratically, as the Framers intended.

We call, therefore, for a new constitutional amendment—an amendment that abolishes life tenure, that strips the federal judiciary of the power to invalidate acts of Congress or state legislatures, and that places the supreme interpretive authority of our fundamental law where it has always belonged: in the Congress, and ultimately, with the American people themselves. Let the Court remain, if you wish, as a court of ordinary law. But it must never again be permitted to govern us from the bench.

To the justices, I say: your borrowed power is forfeit. To the senators who hide behind procedure, I say: the people see you. And to every citizen who has ever felt the sting of disenfranchisement when a Court decision erased your vote, I say: rise. We are not subjects asking for better masters. We are a free people reclaiming our right to rule ourselves.

The Constitution does not belong to the Supreme Court. It belongs to us. Let us take it back. Let us tear down this temple of judicial supremacy and build, in its place, a democracy worthy of the name. The power is ours. The time is now. Let the people govern!

Title: The Marble Temple Must Fall: A Case for Abolishing the Supreme Court and Judicial Review

For over two centuries, the United States has operated under the illusion that a functioning democracy can coexist with a supreme judicial authority possessing the absolute power to nullify the will of the people. We have been taught to revere the Supreme Court as the solemn guardian of our liberties, a neutral arbiter standing above the political fray to protect the Constitution. However, a rigorous examination of history, democratic theory, and modern political reality reveals a stark truth: the Supreme Court and the principle of judicial review are fundamentally incompatible with self-governance. To truly realize the promise of popular sovereignty, the United States must abolish the Supreme Court as it currently exists, eliminate the non-democratic power of judicial review, and return the interpretation of the fundamental law to where it belongs—elected representatives and the citizenry themselves.

The central argument for abolition rests on the bedrock concept of democratic legitimacy. In a republic, power derives from the consent of the governed. Legislators are elected; Presidents are elected; governors and mayors are elected. They are accountable to the people. If they fail, they can be removed. The nine justices of the Supreme Court, conversely, are unelected, unaccountable, and serve life terms. They constitute an oligarchy embedded within a democracy.

The existence of a body of nine individuals—selected increasingly for ideological purity rather than legal acumen—who possess the final word on the most contentious issues of the day is a profound anomaly in a modern democracy. When the Court strikes down a federal law passed by Congress and signed by the President, it is exercising a "counter-majoritarian" force. It is saying to 330 million Americans: "Your representatives were wrong, your votes do not matter, and our opinion outweighs your collective will." While proponents argue this is necessary to protect minority rights against the tyranny of the majority, it invites the far more dangerous reality of the tyranny of the minority. There is no mechanism to check the Court other than the impossible hurdle of a Constitutional amendment. In a system without judicial review, if a law is unpopular or unjust, the people can vote out the lawmakers who passed it. Under the current system, there is no remedy for a nation suffering under a bad judicial decision but to wait for justices to die.

Furthermore, we must dispel the myth that the Court is a non-political institution. The nomination and confirmation process has become the most brutal theater of partisan warfare precisely because everyone understands the stakes: the Court is a super-legislature. From Dobb’s v. Jackson regarding abortion rights to Citizens United regarding campaign finance, and from Bruen regarding gun control to West Virginia v. EPA regarding climate regulation, the Court dictates national policy from the bench. By claiming these are merely "interpretations" of the law, the justices engage in a charade. Legal realism tells us that the personal ideologies and textual preferences of the justices drive outcomes. If the Supreme Court is effectively a third legislative chamber where members serve for forty years and cannot be fired, it should be treated as such—and rejected as a violation of republican principles. We should not tolerate a system where policy is determined by the actuarial tables of octogenarians in robes rather than the ballot box.

Historically, the power of judicial review—the ability to strike down laws as unconstitutional—is not even granted explicitly in the Constitution. It was a power seized by Chief John Marshall in Marbury v. Madison (1803). Thomas Jefferson warned at the time that allowing the judiciary to decide the constitutionality of laws would make the Constitution "a mere thing of wax in the hands of the judiciary, which they may twist and shape into any form they please." Jefferson argued correctly that the Executive and Legislative branches have their own oath to the Constitution and their own right to interpret it. The notion that the Judiciary is the sole or supreme interpreter is a historical accident, not a constitutional imperative. Many thriving democracies, such as the United Kingdom, operate successfully without a supreme judicial veto, relying instead on parliamentary sovereignty where the legislature is the primary guardian of rights.

Critics of abolishing the Court often ask, "Who will protect us?" They fear that without judicial review, the majority will run roughshod over civil liberties. However, this view is deeply pessimistic about the American people and their representatives. It assumes that liberty cannot survive unless enforced by unelected Platonic guardians. In reality, rights are safest when they are politically popular and enshrined in the hearts of the citizenry, not when they depend on the whims of five lawyers in Washington D.C. If a right is so fragile that it requires the protection of an unaccountable court, it is already in danger. Furthermore, elected representatives are capable of protecting rights; indeed, many of our greatest expansions of liberty—from the Civil Rights Act to the Voting Rights Act—were achieved by Congress and the Executive, often dragging the reluctant Court behind.

Abolishing the Supreme Court and judicial review does not mean abandoning the rule of law or the Constitution. Instead, it means adopting a system of Legislative Supremacy or Constitutional Majoritarianism. In this proposed system, the federal judiciary would handle standard legal disputes between parties, contract law, and criminal procedure, but they would lose the power to invalidate statutes passed by Congress. If Congress passes a law, it stands. If the President signs it, it is the law of the land.

Under this model, accountability returns to the political branches. If Congress passes a law restricting free speech or infringing on guns, the people have an immediate remedy: vote them out at the next election. Currently, if Congress passes a law and the Court strikes it down, the voter is powerless. The legislator can blame the Court, and the Court cannot be touched. By stripping the Court of its veto power, we force legislators to take ownership of the constitutionality of their actions. No longer could they pass vague, symbolic laws knowing the Court will clean up the mess; they would bear the full weight of responsibility for their decisions.

Moreover, constitutional interpretation could be formalized through mechanisms of direct democracy or legislative supermajorities. Perhaps a Council of Constitutional Review composed of elected officials, or a requirement that constitutional challenges be settled by a supermajority of the legislature itself, would suffice. The goal is to ensure that those making the rules answer to those living under them.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court and the doctrine of judicial review are relics of a pre-democratic age, vestiges of a distrust in the common person that has outlived its usefulness. They create a government of men, not laws—a government where the men in black robes reign supreme. To secure the future of American democracy, we must dismantle this unelected aristocracy. Let the marble temple fall, and in its place, let us build a system where the Constitution serves the living, not the other way around.

The Case for Abolishing the Supreme Court: Restoring Democratic Sovereignty

The United States Supreme Court, once conceived as a neutral arbiter of the Constitution, has evolved into an institution profoundly at odds with the foundational principle of democratic self-governance. Its exercise of judicial review – the power to invalidate acts of Congress or state legislatures as unconstitutional – represents an anti-democratic anomaly in our system. It is time to abolish the Supreme Court as we know it and eliminate judicial review, transferring the ultimate authority for constitutional interpretation to the elected representatives of the people or directly to the citizenry through mechanisms like constitutional referendums. This radical step is essential to reclaim the sovereignty of the people, ensure genuine accountability, and remedy the deep pathologies plaguing our current judicial supremacy.

1. The Democratic Deficit: An Insoluble Problem of Accountability

The core, irredeemable flaw of the Supreme Court is its complete lack of democratic accountability. Justices are appointed for life, insulated from the will of the electorate after confirmation. They answer to no constituency, face no re-election campaign, and operate largely beyond the reach of public opinion or political consequence. This lifetime tenure, combined with the immense power of judicial review, creates an unelected super-legislature capable of overriding the decisions of democratically elected branches – Congress and state legislatures – often for decades.

Consider the implications: Nine individuals, appointed through an increasingly politicized process, can nullify laws passed by representatives elected by millions. This fundamentally contradicts the principle that government derives its legitimacy from the consent of the governed. As Alexander Bickel famously observed, judicial review is a "deviant institution in the American democracy." Abolishing the Court and eliminating judicial review would finally align constitutional interpretation with democratic legitimacy, ensuring that the meaning of our foundational document evolves through the deliberative choices of representatives directly accountable to the people, or through the direct consent of the governed via carefully constructed amendment or referendum processes.

2. The Myth of Judicial Neutrality and the Reality of Partisanship

The notion that the Supreme Court operates as a purely objective, apolitical interpreter of the Constitution is a dangerous fiction. Justices are nominated and confirmed through an intensely political process, often chosen specifically for their ideological leanings and predictable voting patterns. Recent decades have witnessed the Court become increasingly polarized, issuing landmark decisions along predictable ideological lines that reflect the prevailing winds of partisan politics rather than immutable constitutional principles. Decisions like Citizens United, Shelby County v. Holder, and Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization are stark examples of the Court acting as a political actor, imposing its will on contentious societal issues and effectively amending the Constitution without democratic consent.

Eliminating judicial review removes this avenue for partisan entrenchment by unelected justices. Placing constitutional interpretation in the hands of Congress or state legislatures (subject to judicial protection of specific, enumerated individual rights against legislative infringement) forces these debates into the democratic arena. Elected representatives, facing regular elections, would be compelled to justify their constitutional interpretations to their constituents and build consensus, fostering a more transparent and responsive process reflective of the nation's evolving values.

3. The Tension with Popular Sovereignty and Adaptability

The Constitution begins with "We the People," establishing popular sovereignty as the bedrock of our republic. Judicial review, as exercised by the Supreme Court, fundamentally undermines this principle by allowing an unelected body to overrule the expressed will of the people's representatives. Furthermore, it creates an excessively rigid system. Constitutional amendment, the prescribed democratic method for change, is deliberately difficult. Judicial review, however, allows a simple majority of justices (often appointed by presidents who lost the popular vote) to effectively amend the Constitution through interpretation, bypassing the arduous amendment process and freezing certain interpretations in place for generations. This stifles necessary constitutional evolution and adaptability.

Transferring interpretive authority to elected bodies, operating within a framework that still protects fundamental rights enumerated in the Constitution and Bill of Rights (perhaps with a limited role for courts to enforce those specific guarantees against legislative overreach), allows the Constitution to breathe and adapt more fluidly through democratic means. It empowers each generation to interpret the charter through its elected representatives, ensuring the document remains a living instrument responsive to the needs and values of the contemporary polity.

4. Alternatives: A More Democratic and Accountable System

Abolishing judicial review does not mean abandoning constitutional limits or protections. A reformed system could look like this:

  • Legislative Supremacy (with Safeguards): Congress, as the directly elected branch most representative of the national will, could hold primary authority for interpreting the scope of federal power under the Constitution in most areas. This aligns with the British parliamentary model.
  • Popular Constitutional Amendment/Referendum: For fundamental changes or clarifications to constitutional meaning, the amendment process could be supplemented or streamlined in specific, carefully defined ways, or states could utilize constitutional conventions or referendums to assert interpretations, subject to national consensus requirements.
  • Enumerated Rights Protection: Courts could retain a limited role focused exclusively on protecting specific, clearly defined individual rights explicitly enumerated in the Constitution and Bill of Rights (like those in the First Amendment) against infringement by any branch. This provides a crucial safeguard for minorities while removing courts from broad policy and structural disputes.

Such a system prioritizes democratic decision-making while preserving essential protections against tyranny. It forces constitutional debates into the open democratic arena, where elected officials must justify their positions to the voters who can hire or fire them.

Conclusion

The United States Supreme Court, wielding the anti-democratic power of judicial review, stands as a significant impediment to genuine popular sovereignty. Its lack of accountability, inherent politicization, and rigid control over constitutional evolution are incompatible with the democratic ideals upon which this nation was founded. While abolishing the Court and ending judicial review is a profound step, it is a necessary one to restore power to the people and their elected representatives. It replaces rule by an unaccountable judicial oligarchy with democratic deliberation and accountability. By vesting ultimate constitutional authority in Congress or the people themselves through democratic processes, we can create a system more faithful to the principle that government derives its just powers from the consent of the governed. The time has come to dismantle this undemocratic institution and build a system where the Constitution is interpreted by, and for, the people it serves.
